observations.text: Sure, that's fine. What would you like to know?

The process starts when a customer sends us a request for a quotation. We take that request, check the customer’s information in our CRM, and then create the quotation in our quoting system using the customer and pricing information. Once it’s ready, we send the quotation to the customer by email. The whole point is to produce an accurate quotation for the customer.

That would be me, and the other sales staff in our team. We all handle the quotation requests from start to finish—recording the request, checking the customer info, creating the quotation, and sending it out.

Yes, it’s a separate step. When a customer sends us a request, we log it into our system—basically, we note down the details of the request so there’s a record of it. After that, we move on to checking the customer’s information in the CRM and then creating the quotation.

There is one exception, actually. If the quotation amount is over 1,000,000 yen, we need to get approval from a manager before we can send it to the customer. That approval is for credit risk management. Otherwise, the process is pretty straightforward.

Checking the customer’s information in the CRM is important because we need to make sure we have the correct details—like their contact information and any relevant history—so that the quotation we prepare is accurate and goes to the right person. If we skipped that step, we might end up sending a quotation with outdated or incorrect information, which could cause problems for the customer and for us.

Recording the request is necessary because it gives us a clear record of what the customer asked for and when. If we didn’t record it, we could lose track of the request, forget details, or have no way to follow up or refer back to it later. It helps keep things organized and ensures we don’t miss anything.

Creating the quotation in the quoting system is necessary because that’s where we generate the actual document with the correct pricing and customer details. If we didn’t create it there, we wouldn’t have a proper, standardized quotation to send to the customer, and it would be much harder to keep track of or reference later. It’s the core step that produces the final output.

Sending the quotation by email is necessary because that’s how the customer actually receives the document. Without that step, the whole process wouldn’t be complete—the customer wouldn’t get the pricing information they asked for. The overall purpose of the whole process is to produce an accurate quotation and get it to the customer.

The manager approval is required by our internal process—it’s a standard step we follow for quotations over 1,000,000 yen. If the manager doesn’t approve it, then we wouldn’t be able to send the quotation to the customer. We’d have to hold it or go back to the customer or the manager to sort things out, but I don’t have details beyond that.

Receiving the customer’s request is necessary because that’s what starts the whole process. Without it, we wouldn’t know what the customer needs, and there would be nothing to work on. If we didn’t receive the request, we simply wouldn’t be able to prepare or send a quotation.

As for other conditions or exceptions, the only one I can think of is the manager approval for quotations over 1,000,000 yen. I don’t know of any other special cases beyond that.
